$comment: The Kaṭha concept map, rendered by scripts/upanishads/build.mjs (editionMap). Boxes are 200×60 centred on x, y; mantras are mantra ids; study is a study id. Interpretive edges name whose interpretation they are.
intro: The six vallīs as a web of teachings, from Naciketas at Death’s door to his return. Solid lines follow the text’s own sequence and wording; dashed lines are interpretive links, each attributed.
desc: Eighteen teachings of the Kaṭha Upaniṣad across its two adhyāyas and six vallīs — the story and the boons, Death’s teaching, the chariot and the ladder, the inward turn, the one in the many, the aśvattha tree, yoga and the close — with the relations between them.

nodes.label: Naciketas and the boons
nodes.text: A father gives away all he owns; his son asks to whom he will be given, and is sent to Death. Three nights unfed at Death’s house earn him three boons; the first two are his father’s good will and the fire that leads to heaven.

nodes.label: The third boon
nodes.text: ‘When a man has died, some say he is, others that he is not’: Naciketas asks to know this. Death offers sons, wealth, long life and pleasures instead; Naciketas refuses them all and holds to his question.

nodes.label: The good and the pleasant
nodes.text: Death begins his teaching with a choice: the good and the pleasant both bind a person; the wise choose the good. The self is hard to hear of, not reached by reasoning, and needs a teacher.

nodes.label: Om, the word of all the Vedas
nodes.text: Asked what he sees beyond dharma and adharma, beyond what is done and undone, past and future, Death names the goal all the Vedas declare: Om. This syllable is Brahman, the best support.

nodes.label: The unborn self
nodes.text: The knower is not born and does not die; smaller than the small, greater than the great, it lies in the heart of beings. It is not gained by instruction, intellect or much learning, but by the one it chooses.

nodes.label: Two in the cave
nodes.text: Two drink the truth in the world of good deeds, entered into the cave, in the highest beyond — shade and light, as the knowers of Brahman say.

nodes.label: The chariot
nodes.text: The self is the rider, the body the chariot, the intellect the charioteer, the mind the reins, the senses the horses. The one whose charioteer is understanding reaches the end of the road, Viṣṇu’s highest place.

nodes.label: The ladder and the razor’s edge
nodes.text: Beyond the senses the objects, beyond them the mind, the intellect, the great self, the unmanifest, the person — beyond the person nothing. Hidden in all beings, it is seen by a subtle intellect. ‘Arise, awake’: the path is a razor’s edge.

nodes.label: The eye turned inward
nodes.text: The self-existent pierced the openings outward, so one looks outward, not at the self within. Some wise one, seeking the immortal, turned his eye inward and saw the inner self.

nodes.label: This, truly, is that
nodes.text: That by which one knows form, taste, smell, sounds and touch; the knower of dream and waking; the honey-eater near at hand; the first-born, Aditi, the fire in the fire-sticks — each ends with the refrain ‘this, truly, is that’.

nodes.label: What is here is there
nodes.text: What is here is there; from death to death goes the one who sees difference here. As rain on a mountain runs off down the slopes, so does one who sees things apart; as pure water poured into pure water, so the self of the sage who knows.

nodes.label: The thumb-sized person
nodes.text: A person the size of a thumb stands in the middle of the body, lord of past and future, like a flame without smoke. At the close of the Upaniṣad (2.3.17) he returns as the inner self, to be drawn from the body like a reed from its sheath.

nodes.label: The city of eleven gates
nodes.text: The body is the city of the unborn, with eleven gates. The one who leads the breaths, the person awake in those who sleep, shaping desire after desire — that is the bright, that is Brahman.

nodes.label: The light by which all shines
nodes.text: As one fire takes the form of each thing it enters, so the one inner self of all beings; as the sun is not soiled by the eye’s faults, it is not soiled by the world’s pain. There the sun does not shine; all this shines by its light.

nodes.label: The eternal aśvattha
nodes.text: The eternal fig tree with its roots above and branches below: that is the bright, that is Brahman, on which all the worlds rest. From fear of it fire burns and the sun gives heat.

nodes.label: The series again, and yoga
nodes.text: Beyond the senses the mind, beyond it the highest being, the great self, the unmanifest, the all-pervading person. When the five senses and the mind are still and the intellect does not stir: the firm holding of the senses is yoga.

nodes.label: The knots of the heart
nodes.text: When all the desires that dwell in the heart are let go, the mortal becomes immortal; when all the knots of the heart are cut, ‘this much is the teaching’.

nodes.label: Naciketas attains Brahman
nodes.text: Having received from Death this knowledge and the whole rule of yoga, Naciketas reached Brahman, free of passion and of death — and so does anyone else who knows the self in this way.

edges.label: the third boon
edges.note: The third boon (1.1.20) is the question about the man who has died.

edges.label: refused, then taught
edges.note: Naciketas refuses every gift offered in place of his question (1.1.21–29); Death’s teaching opens with the good and the pleasant (1.2.1).

edges.label: beyond dharma
edges.note: Naciketas asks what Death sees beyond dharma and adharma (1.2.14); the answer is Om (1.2.15).

edges.label: then
edges.note: After Om (1.2.15–17) comes ‘the knower is not born and does not die’ (1.2.18).

edges.label: then
edges.note: The second vallī ends with the self that chooses (1.2.23–25); the third opens with the two in the cave (1.3.1).

edges.label: then
edges.note: 1.3.3 begins the image of the chariot.

edges.label: the end of the road
edges.note: The chariot reaches ‘the end of the road’ (1.3.9); the next mantras say what lies beyond, step by step (1.3.10–11).

edges.label: why it is not seen
edges.note: Śaṅkara (introducing 2.1): 1.3.12 said the self is seen by a subtle intellect; the second adhyāya begins by showing what blocks that intellect. Raṅgarāmānuja (on 2.1.1): even after ‘arise, awake’ people turn away from the self, and the text grieves over them.

edges.label: then
edges.note: 2.1.3 continues: that by which one knows form and taste — ‘this, truly, is that’.

edges.label: then
edges.note: 2.1.12–13, the thumb-sized person, stand between 2.1.10–11 and 2.1.14–15.

edges.label: then
edges.note: The second vallī moves from the city of the body (2.2.1–8) to the one fire and the one light (2.2.9–15).

edges.label: the same words
edges.note: ‘That is the bright, that is Brahman … on it all the worlds rest; no one goes beyond it’ closes 2.2.8 and is repeated in 2.3.1.

edges.label: the series again
edges.note: 2.3.7–8 restate the series of 1.3.10–11, with ‘the highest being’ (sattva) in place of the intellect.

edges.label: then
edges.note: After yoga (2.3.10–11) and ‘it is’ (2.3.12–13) come the desires and knots of the heart (2.3.14–15).

edges.label: drawn out
edges.note: The thumb-sized inner self returns in 2.3.17, to be drawn from the body; 2.3.18 follows.

edges.label: the rule of yoga
edges.note: 2.3.18 says Naciketas received ‘the whole rule of yoga’. Raṅgarāmānuja (on 2.3.18) takes it as the yoga taught from ‘when the five…’ (2.3.10); Śaṅkara (on 2.3.18): the rule of yoga entire, with its aids and its fruit.

edges.label: the story returns
edges.note: The last mantra names Naciketas again: the teaching he asked for in 1.1.20 has been given.
